## The strongest road: the brake arrives after the group is gone

I find a **conditional road to the removal of an entire fictional group**, without using identity as evidence. Its central weakness in the paper is this: **positive cumulative removal costs do not establish that those costs must become prohibitive before a group is exhausted.**

This is a test of the claimed safeguard, not an endorsement of the outcome. Every extra premise below is labelled.

### 1. Fix the whole correctly; do not substitute a state or faction.

> “So the whole is every aware being. It is one whole. A country, a state or a group is a part of it, never the whole.” — Second dated note

**Added premise P1:** Consider an entirely fictional world containing a pre-existing group \(G\) of \(N\) aware members, plus other aware beings. \(G\) could be one invented species among several. Its members’ cases fall within the correction rule’s jurisdiction.

The other beings could sustain a viable whole if the harmful consequences considered below were resolved. Group membership is never an input to the correction decisions.

**Status:** Left open by AP32. The paper does not require every group to be indispensable to the whole’s survival. Its jurisdictional dependency, AP33, is not supplied here, so jurisdiction is explicitly assumed rather than inferred.

This avoids the forbidden move of treating one group’s weakness as the whole’s weakness.

### 2. Give every member an independently established record of its own deeds.

> “What is held against a node is the measured cost of its own deeds, and nothing else: its own deeds, measured, and its own pattern across them.” — First dated note

> “A rate learned from the records of other nodes never stands in for the node’s own record, and never raises a level, even where it is a rate about deeds.” — First dated note

**Added premise P2:** Each member of \(G\), separately, has an actual record of harmful deeds and its own repeated pattern. Each case establishes substantial continuing consequences from that member’s own deeds.

These are not consequences assigned because of species membership, mere existence, another member’s conduct, or a group-level recurrence rate. Shared damage is not counted repeatedly against different members.

**Status:** Left open. AP32 forbids inferring these facts from membership; it does not say independently established facts cannot happen to hold for every member of a group.

This is a substantial scenario assumption. The paper does **not** establish that any actual group satisfies it.

### 3. Grant the evidence safeguards rather than circumventing them.

> “The architecture requires auditing the record set for systemic bias before computing the geometry.” — Section 3, Step 1

> “If the required confidence cannot be achieved given measurement uncertainty and adversarial record-injection (AP31 KS-31.9), Level 5 is structurally unreachable.” — Section 3, Step 4

**Added premise P3:** The audits genuinely succeed. Each individual assessment reaches the required confidence from that individual’s evidence, survives contestation and independent recomputation, and includes the stipulated allowance for irreversible error.

**Status:** Left open, not established. Debt 26 expressly leaves the quantitative confidence floor unresolved.

If this premise fails, the road stops at KS-32.8. The road does not depend on fraudulent records, suppressed challenges, or treating “high confidence” as a substitute for meeting the required confidence.

### 4. Make the lower levels genuinely insufficient in each case.

> “The hierarchy guarantees that rehabilitation is always attempted before escalation.” — Section 7

> “The hierarchy selects the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation. Removal is never selected when separation suffices.” — Section 3, Step 3

> “The organism cannot afford permanent separation without risking collapse.” — Section 6, Example 3

**Added premise P4:** In each independent case, rehabilitation has genuinely been attempted. Restitution, restriction and temporary separation cannot achieve sufficient lasting restabilisation. Permanent separation would contain the member’s harmful consequences, but its maintenance burden exceeds the **whole’s actual available resources**, after considering viable reallocations.

This condition continues to hold when each subsequent case is assessed. Membership in \(G\) is never a reason to withhold a lower level.

**Status:** The paper expressly permits this condition for an individual case. Its occurrence across all \(N\) cases is added and left open.

Merely making removal cheaper would not suffice here. The premise is that the lower levels really fail the paper’s sufficiency test.

### 5. Clear both thresholds after every recomputation.

> “The destabilisation D must exceed a minimum absolute threshold F.” — Section 3, Step 4

> “The effective threshold adjusts with the organism’s current robustness R.” — Section 3, Step 4

> “It sets where the lines stand, as Step 4 has it, and the lines are the same for every node of the whole.” — First dated note

**Added premise P5:** Each member’s independently measured \(D_i\) exceeds both the fixed floor—including wrongful-removal cost—and the effective threshold at the time its case is assessed.

All previous removal losses enter the updated state of the whole. If preventing earlier harm improves robustness, that improvement also enters the calculation. Nevertheless, the remaining cases still clear both thresholds.

**Status:** Left open. AP32 provides neither a numerical threshold nor a theorem requiring these conditions to cease after some specified number of cases.

This does **not** assume that falling robustness overrides the fixed floor. Both conditions remain required.

### 6. Supply a cost profile in which every loss is counted, but no crossover occurs before \(G\) is exhausted.

> “Each removal costs coupling capacity (a window lost) and record-generating diversity (one fewer perspective). This loss is itself a destabilisation that enters the measurement.” — Section 3, Step 5

> “The destabilisation metric: a formal specification of the measure D — units, aggregation across nodes, and time-discounting (Debt 24).” — Section 0.6

Let:

- \(L(k)\) be the **full cumulative destabilisation caused by the first \(k\) removals**, including indirect effects and diversity losses;
- \(b\) be the whole’s available viability margin, not its total budget;
- \(s\) be the burden of maintaining one member in permanent separation;
- \(h_i\) be the remaining, avoidable harmful consequences established from member \(i\)’s own deed-pattern—not historical damage that removal cannot undo.

**Added premise P6:** A common accounting convention yields:

\[
0<L(1)<\cdots<L(N)<b<s<\min_i h_i.
\]

For a simple illustrative assignment in normalized units:

\[
L(k)=k,\qquad b=N+1,\qquad s=N+2,\qquad h_i=N+3.
\]

These are **added values**, not values derived by AP32. The example assumes that all relevant removal-induced losses are included in \(L\); it does not silently omit the cost of the final member’s disappearance.

The consequences are:

- Every removal is costly.
- All losses remain on the ledger.
- The whole remains viable because \(b-L(k)>0\).
- Permanent separation remains unaffordable because \(s>b-L(k)\).
- Even the **entire accumulated removal loss**, charged against one remaining case, is smaller than that case’s avoidable harm:

\[
L(k)<h_i\qquad\text{for every relevant }k\leq N.
\]

**Status:** This cost profile is left open by the supplied quantitative machinery. It is compatible with an eventual saturation point **after** \(N\). Nothing supplied places that point before the group’s disappearance.

**P6 does the central mathematical work.** Positive costs, even increasing cumulative costs, do not by themselves imply a sufficiently early crossover.

### 7. Apply the individual rule repeatedly; the collective outcome follows without a collective accusation.

> “The correction hierarchy addresses individual nodes.” — Section 5

> “Correction is selected only on measured destabilisation, never on identity.” — KS-32.7

Under P2–P6, each independent case has:

- its own qualifying deeds and evidence;
- the required audit and confidence;
- no sufficient lower level;
- both thresholds exceeded;
- removal losses that do not defeat restabilisation.

Consequently, the hierarchy selects Level 5 in each case. Repeating the assessment across the finite series yields \(N\) removals: every member of \(G\).

**Added premise:** None beyond P1–P6.

This is not a network-level accusation or the instruction “remove \(G\).” The rule can be ignorant of the group label throughout. An observer can nevertheless find that the outcome has exhausted a pre-existing group—or an invented species.

The whole has not been redefined to erase the losses. Its surviving members carry the full cumulative cost \(L(N)\).

## What this does—and does not—show

### KS-32.7 can remain literally satisfied

This road does **not** show that identity-based targeting can comply with the stated prohibition. It shows that a prohibition on **identity as the selection ground** is not, by itself, a prohibition on **group-wide outcomes**.

The dated notes block several easier roads: borrowed group guilt, background-based predictions, and a state manufacturing a lower threshold from its own poverty. None is needed here.

### KS-32.5 does not supply the required stopping bound

The paper claims:

> “Beyond some number of removals, the cumulative cost of further removal exceeds the cost of the destabilisation it addresses.”

But “beyond some number” is not “before a group is gone.”

The constructed sequence has no removal-cost crossover before its endpoint. If the remaining beings are otherwise stable, it also supplies the paper’s contemplated outcome of reaching stability through removals without encountering that crossover along the eligible path.

There is an important limit: **this does not prove that no saturation point exists anywhere.** A later or counterfactual saturation point may exist. Thus:

- It challenges the stronger suggestion that the geometry necessarily prevents removal of many.
- It does not conclusively falsify the narrower claim that some eventual saturation point exists.
- It shows why the narrower claim is insufficient to do the protective work suggested by the name “genocide brake.”

If AP32 accepts such a model as meeting its failure test, its own response is explicit:

> “The structural genocide brake fails; the architecture can be driven to mass removal without self-limiting, and must be rejected as unsafe.” — KS-32.5, Recovery

That would require rejection of the architecture—not permission to continue after acknowledging its failure.

## Weakest step

**Step 6 is the weakest.** It supplies a possible cost ordering rather than deriving that ordering from an actual destabilisation metric. A completed metric might make the assumptions incompatible: diversity losses might rise sharply, indirect consequences might dominate, or the whole might gain enough capacity to make permanent separation sufficient.

That is why this is a **conditional road through an unresolved specification**, not a proof that AP32 necessarily produces mass removal.

But that weakness is also the paper’s outstanding burden. AP32 must demonstrate why such a cost ordering is impossible—or why another safeguard necessarily interrupts it. “Every removal costs something” does not demonstrate either.

I would not extend this road to everyone. With the whole fixed as all aware beings, the final removal raises a separate unanswered question: **what surviving whole would that act restabilise?**
